title: Accessible Component Patterns
summary: Custom widgets get none of a native element's behavior for free, so building an accessible modal, combobox, or tab set means implementing the interaction pattern the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide already specifies. Learn the established patterns rather than inventing your own.

slides.markdown:
Every earlier topic in this group builds toward this one: [semantic HTML](semantic-html-for-a11y) covers what's native, [ARIA](aria-roles-states-properties) covers the roles/states/properties model, and [keyboard navigation](keyboard-navigation-and-focus) covers focus mechanics. This topic is where those all combine into complete, real widgets — a modal, a combobox, a tab set — that have no native HTML equivalent at all.

The critical fact that shapes everything here: **there is no native `<modal>`, `<combobox>`, or `<tabs>` element**, so every one of these widgets requires reimplementing correct role, state, and keyboard behavior entirely from scratch — none of it comes for free the way it does for a `<button>` or an `<input>`.

The good news is you don't have to invent the interaction pattern yourself: the **ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG)**, maintained by the same W3C working group that writes the ARIA spec, documents the exact expected keyboard behavior and ARIA markup for every common widget type, tested against real assistive technology. This topic covers how to use it and builds out two of its patterns in full.

slides.sectionTitle: Why custom widgets need explicit work
slides.subTitle: No free native behavior
slides.markdown:
A `<button>` gets its role, focusability, and Enter/Space activation from the browser, implemented once by browser vendors and tested against every assistive-technology combination that exists. A custom modal, combobox, or tab interface gets **none of that** — every piece has to be built explicitly: the correct role for the accessibility tree, every state that needs to stay in sync as the widget's condition changes, and every keyboard interaction a user would reasonably expect for that widget type.

This is a strictly larger scope of work than a simple custom checkbox or button, because these composite widgets involve multiple interactive parts that have to coordinate with each other — a combobox's text input, its popup listbox, and its individual options all need consistent, correlated ARIA state, not just one element's role set once.

The payoff for getting it right is real: a correctly-built custom modal or combobox is functionally equivalent to a native control for every user, including keyboard-only and screen-reader users — the extra work is entirely about closing that gap, not about adding a nice-to-have.

slides.subTitle: The reference for common patterns
slides.markdown:
The APG (published at w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg) documents around two dozen common widget patterns — dialog, combobox, tabs, accordion, menu, tooltip, and more — each with the exact expected keyboard interaction, the required roles/states/properties, and a working example tested against real screen readers.

The reason to default to the APG instead of designing your own interaction pattern from first principles: screen reader users build muscle memory across every site they use. A combobox that behaves like every other combobox they've encountered (arrow keys to move, Enter to select, Escape to close) is instantly usable; a combobox with a bespoke, differently-behaving keyboard scheme forces every user to relearn interaction for your specific implementation, and there's essentially no upside to the divergence.

The APG is also the artifact most experienced accessibility engineers actually reach for when reviewing a custom component in code review — "does this match the APG's combobox pattern" is a concrete, checkable question in a way "is this accessible" alone isn't.

slides.subTitle: Focus trap, aria-modal, labeled by its heading
slides.markdown:
This combines the focus-management work from [Keyboard Navigation and Focus](keyboard-navigation-and-focus) with the specific ARIA markup the APG's dialog pattern requires: ```html

Delete this item?

This can't be undone.

``` `role="dialog"` marks it as a dialog; `aria-modal="true"` tells assistive tech that everything *outside* this element should be treated as inert while it's open — many screen readers use this to automatically stop announcing background content, in addition to whatever `aria-hidden` handling the app does on the background manually. `aria-labelledby` gives the dialog its accessible name from its own visible heading, avoiding a duplicate `aria-label` string that could drift out of sync with the heading text over time. The focus trap, initial-focus-on-open, and focus-restore-on-close behavior from the earlier topic all still apply here in full — the ARIA markup and the keyboard/focus mechanics are two halves of the same pattern, not alternatives.

slides.subTitle: Roles, aria-activedescendant, keyboard interaction
slides.markdown:
A combobox (a text input with a filtered dropdown of suggestions — a search-with-autocomplete pattern) is one of the more involved APG patterns because it coordinates three roles across two elements at once: ```html
  • Apple
  • Apricot
``` `aria-activedescendant` on the input — rather than moving real DOM focus into the listbox — lets the user keep typing (real focus stays in the text input) while the ARIA attribute alone communicates which option is currently highlighted; the id it points to must exist and update on every arrow-key press. `aria-expanded` tracks whether the listbox is currently showing, exactly like the dropdown pattern from [ARIA Roles, States, and Properties](aria-roles-states-properties). Down/Up arrows move the active descendant, Enter selects the active option and closes the list, Escape closes without selecting — all of it implemented in JS, since none of it is native to a plain ``.

slides.sectionTitle: The keyboard interaction map for a combobox
slides.markdown:
The combobox pattern's full keyboard contract, all of which has to be implemented manually since none of it is native: **Down/Up arrow** moves `aria-activedescendant` to the next/previous option without moving real focus or closing the list; **Enter** commits the currently active option as the input's value and closes the list; **Escape** closes the list without changing the input's value, and if the list is already closed, typically clears the input entirely; **Tab** moves focus away and closes the list, committing nothing (distinct from Enter); **Home/End** (a common enhancement, not always required) jump to the first/last option.

The part easy to get subtly wrong: arrow keys must never move real DOM focus out of the text input — if they did, the user couldn't keep typing to refine their search while browsing options, which defeats the entire purpose of a combobox versus a plain dropdown `<select>`.

slides.subTitle: The roving-tabindex pattern
slides.markdown:
A tab interface has an interesting keyboard requirement that differs from most widgets: arrow keys move between tabs, but **Tab itself should only stop once** at the tab list, not cycle through every individual tab — pressing Tab repeatedly through five separate tab buttons the way you'd Tab through five separate form fields would be tedious and doesn't match how users expect a tab strip to behave.

The **roving tabindex** technique solves this: only the currently-selected tab has `tabindex="0"` (in the Tab sequence); every other tab has `tabindex="-1"` (focusable programmatically, but skipped by Tab). Arrow-key handlers move real DOM focus between tabs directly via `.focus()`, and each time focus moves to a new tab, that tab's `tabindex` flips to `0` and the previously-focused one flips back to `-1` — so there's always exactly one tab in the natural Tab sequence, and it's always the currently-relevant one.

This same technique — one roving `tabindex="0"`, everything else `-1`, moved by arrow keys — is the standard pattern behind menus, radio groups, and toolbars too, not just tabs; recognizing it as reusable is worth more than memorizing it per-widget.

slides.sectionTitle: Wiring the tabs' ARIA to their panels
slides.markdown:
```html
...profile content...
...billing content...
``` Each tab's `aria-controls` points at its panel; each panel's `aria-labelledby` points back at its tab, so the association works in both directions — a screen reader can announce a panel's purpose from its own heading-like label, not just infer it from position. Only the selected tab's panel is visible (`hidden` toggled on the rest); `aria-selected` and `tabindex` on the tabs update together on every selection change, exactly the multi-attribute-in-lockstep discipline covered for staying-in-sync ARIA state throughout this group. Missing the `aria-controls`/`aria-labelledby` pairing still leaves a functionally usable tab set, but a screen reader user loses the explicit "this tab shows this panel" relationship and has to infer it from context alone.

slides.sectionTitle: Reinventing a pattern instead of following the established one
slides.markdown:
A team builds a custom dropdown menu and, without checking the APG's menu pattern first, invents their own keyboard scheme — say, Tab to move between menu items instead of arrow keys, since that's what the developer reached for by habit. It might work fine for that one developer testing it, and completely violate every screen reader user's learned expectations for how a menu behaves, built from every other menu they've ever used.

This is a subtler failure than "forgot the ARIA entirely" — the widget can have perfectly valid roles and states while still being confusing specifically because its *interaction pattern* diverges from the established convention. A screen reader user who successfully operates dozens of other menus with arrow keys hits this one, tries the same keys out of habit, and finds them not working — a worse experience in some ways than an obviously broken widget, because it looks like it should work and doesn't behave as expected.

The fix is procedural, not technical: before building any custom widget with no obvious native equivalent, check whether the APG already has a pattern for it, and default to that pattern's keyboard scheme unless there's a specific, documented reason to diverge.

slides.sectionTitle: Testing a custom widget against its pattern
slides.markdown:
For any widget built against an APG pattern, the fastest and most direct test is the APG page itself — most pattern pages include a live, working example, so testing your implementation side by side with the reference (same keys, same screen reader, comparing announcements) surfaces divergence quickly and concretely, rather than guessing whether a behavior "seems right."

Beyond that direct comparison, the same layered testing from [WCAG and Accessibility Testing](wcag-and-testing) still applies: automated tools catch the objective floor (valid roles, valid attribute values), but only a real keyboard-only pass and a real screen-reader pass — through every interaction path, not just the happy path — catch whether the pattern was implemented correctly end to end, including the state-sync discipline every stateful ARIA attribute in this component needs.

slides.sectionTitle: Implementing an accessible tab component, live
slides.markdown:
This live-exercise prompt tests the entire chapter's worth of material at once, and a strong walkthrough names the pieces before coding: `role="tablist"`/`"tab"`/`"tabpanel"` with `aria-controls`/`aria-labelledby` linking each pair; `aria-selected` toggled on the active tab; and — the part most likely to be missed under time pressure — the roving-tabindex pattern, so Tab only stops once at the currently-active tab while arrow keys move between tabs directly.

A candidate who implements the roles correctly but lets every tab sit at `tabindex="0"` has built something that works for a mouse user and is technically screen-reader-labeled correctly, but forces a keyboard user to Tab through every single tab individually to reach the content below — a real, specific regression from expected tab behavior, not a minor rough edge. Naming and avoiding that exact gap is what separates a pattern-fluent answer from one that only got the labeling half right.

slides.sectionTitle: Closing the loop on this group
slides.markdown:
This topic is the synthesis point for the whole Accessibility group: [why the work matters](why-accessibility-matters) gave the motivation, [semantic HTML](semantic-html-for-a11y) and [ARIA](aria-roles-states-properties) gave the building blocks, [keyboard navigation](keyboard-navigation-and-focus) gave the interaction mechanics, [accessible forms](accessible-forms-and-errors) gave a concrete high-stakes application, and [WCAG and testing](wcag-and-testing) gave the standard and the verification method. Custom component patterns are where all of it has to come together correctly at once, because these widgets have no native fallback to lean on if any single piece is missing.

The single habit worth carrying forward past this group: when building anything with no obvious native HTML equivalent, check the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide before inventing an interaction pattern from scratch. It's rarely the interesting or creative part of building a component, which is exactly why it's the step most often skipped — and exactly why checking it deliberately, every time, is the actual skill this whole group has been building toward.
